#4785. The Correlation Between Sports and Suicide

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

The list of professional athletes who have killed themselves is long. It includes all-pro football players Junior Seau, Mike Webster, and Jim Tyrer; “Miracle on Ice” hockey star Mark Pavelich; Olympic beach volleyball medalist Mike Whitmarsh; Olympic freestyle skiing medalist Jeret Peterson; Olympic women’s cycling medalist Kelly Catlin; pro golfer Erica Blasberg; Cy Young Award winner Mike Flanagan; Yankees pitcher Hideki Irabu; and Angels pitcher Donnie Moore.

One reason why athletes have a high risk of suicide is that people who have enjoyed adulation and success throughout their young lives sometimes have a hard time adjusting when their playing days end. The roar of the crowd is gone, the adrenaline rush that accompanies top-level competition is no longer there, big paychecks most likely have ceased, locker room camaraderie is absent, and trainers and agents aren’t around to provide round-the-clock personal care. Most athletes who leave the game are still young by professional standards, whereas others in their 30s have begun to establish them­selves in long-term careers; athletes are just starting out and may not be prepared for life after sports.

According to one university researcher, 77 former Major League Baseball players have killed themselves. More than half were between their late 20s and late 40s, when their absence from the game was the most pronounced and future plans were uncertain, leading the researcher to recommend that MLB players receive counseling after they retire.[1]

Another factor is that many professional athletes leave the game with beat-up bodies. They were in peak physical shape when they first started playing, but overuse of joints and muscles plus injuries have taken a toll, mentally as well as physically. It’s hard to say goodbye to the limelight, but even harder sometimes to adjust to life afterward—chronic pain, decreased mobility, and—if they have suffered concussions—possible and permanent brain impairment.

In recent years, the results of studies on CTE—brain degeneration caused by repeated head trauma—have raised troubling concerns. At this time, there isn’t an accurate diagnostic test for CTE in living brains—it can only be found postmortem—but Chris Nowinski, a behavioral bio-scientist who played football in college, says that 99 percent of former NFL players whose brains have been examined posthumously have had CTE, and more than a few have died by suicide.[2]

Horse racing presents its own challenges. First and most obviously, it’s extremely dangerous. According to the president and CEO of the Jockey’s Guild, two jockeys die each year, on average, from racing, and 60 others are paralyzed. The concussions that jockeys get from falling off a horse at high speeds are as violent as the collisions of football players, and jockeys wear less protective gear. Add to this the challenge of maintaining a low weight, which results in eating disorders, plus frequent criticism from owners, trainers, and bettors, and it’s not surprising that jockeys suffer a variety of mental health issues. Three years ago, the horse racing world was stunned by the suicides of two jockeys. One of them was a friend of Mike Smith, who won the Triple Crown in 2018 at the age of 52 and is in the Racing Hall of Fame. Smith said that he knew other riders who killed themselves. “This is not all of a sudden just happening,” he said. “It’s been going on. You just never heard of it.”[3]

To date, only one female athlete has been diagnosed with CTE—a former Australian rules football player who played seven games in 2017, retired later that year, and killed herself in 2022 at age 28. Her family donated her brain to the Australian Sports Brain Bank, and the director there reported that he found “multiple CTE lesions.”[4] Here in the United States, two former World Cup stars, Brandi Chastain and Michelle Akers, have expressed public concern over memory-loss issues after they retired, and said that they will participate in a CTE study at Boston University.

Players and former players aren’t the only people at risk of suicide, however. Studies show that when a city’s most popular sports teams win a national championship, there is a temporary decline in the suicide rate. Conversely, after a loss, the rate goes up.

The U.S. men’s hockey team’s 1980 Olympic victory over the Soviet Union—the so-called “Miracle on Ice”—came at a time when the Iran hostage crisis had gone on for 111 days, and Russia’s invasion of Afghanistan was a month old. Millions of people in America had never seen a hockey game, didn’t know the rules or the names of any of the players, yet were glued to their TV sets and radios, cheering the home team to victory. It’s not surprising that the U.S. suicide rate was unusually low that day, February 22, 1980, compared with other February 22nds in the 20 years before and 20 years after.[5] (It may have been unusually high in the Soviet Union, although there are no data available to verify this.)

Suicide expert Thomas Joiner, who conducted that study, has conducted other studies that show a link between the success or failure of a sports team and suicide. For example, he found that fewer suicides occur on Sundays in America when the Super Bowl is played than on other Sundays during the year. Also, he determined that there is a correlation between the suicide rate and the national rankings of the football team at Florida State University, where Joiner is a tenured professor, and Ohio State University, which is a perennial football powerhouse. When the team was highly ranked, the suicide rate in the two cities—Gainesville and Columbus, respectively—was lower, Joiner found.[6]

Other studies support this. In one study of 30 metropolitan areas in the U.S. over 20 years, researchers noted that the suicide rate went down when the area’s pro team made the playoffs and went on to win a champion­ship.[7] Conversely, the defeat of a high-profile soccer team in England led to increased cases of self-poisoning, according to a different study.[8] In a third study, suicides of young men increased in Quebec when the Montreal Canadiens hockey team lost an early-round playoff series.[9]

People joke about “living and dying” with their favorite team, but the sense of belongingness that someone feels rooting for a team can be undone when that team loses and its season is over. It’s easy to say that no one should take sports so seriously, but as a fan myself, I’m aware of the lure.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

[1] Torre, Pablo S. “A Light in the Darkness,” Sports Illustrated, June 21, 2010.

[2] Nowinski, Chris. “Troubling Trend,” Sports Illustrated, July 16, 2018.

[3] Whyno, Stephen. “Weight Watching, Injury Dangers, Caustic Feedback Add to Mental Health Woes for Horseracing Jockeys,” Associated Press, May 23, 2023.

[4] ESPN News Services. “Heather Anderson Diagnosed with CTE in 1st Case for Female Athlete,” July 4, 2023.

[5] Joiner, Thomas. Why People Die by Suicide, 130-1.

[6] Joiner, Thomas. Why People Die by Suicide, 130.

[7] Fernquist, R.M. “An Aggregate Analysis of Professional Sports, Suicide, and Homicide Rates, 30 Metropolitan Area, 1971-1990,” Aggression and Violent Behavior, 2000, p. 329-341.

[8] Steels, M.D. “Deliberate Self-Poisoning—Nottingham Forest Football Club and F.A. Defeat,” Irish Journal of Psychological Medicine, 1994, p. 76-78.

[9] Trovato, F. “The Stanley Cup of Hockey and Suicide in Quebec, 1951-1992,” Social Forces, 1998, p. 105-126.

#4784. Switching from GLP-1 Injections to Wegovy Pill Shows Additional Weight Loss of 4.1%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People with overweight or obesity who switch from an injectable GLP-1 medication to the Wegovy (semaglutide) pill may continue to lose weight, according to findings from the OCTANE study presented at the 2026 Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy.

The study is among the first real-world analyses to examine weight loss and treatment experiences among people who switched from an injectable weight loss medication to oral semaglutide (Wegovy).

However, while real-world studies like this can provide useful insights into how treatments work in everyday life, these findings do not prove that switching to the Wegovy pill caused the weight loss.

The results have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

This was a retrospective cohort analysis evaluating weight change, treatment adherence, and patient satisfaction after people switched from injectable semaglutide (Wegovy) or tirzepatide (Zepbound) to oral semaglutide for weight management.

The study included a random sample of 194 adults with overweight or obesity and at least one obesity-related complication, such as hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnea, and dyslipidemia.

Participants had no history of diabetes or bariatric surgery and had an average baseline weight of 221.6 pounds (100.5 kg) and an average body mass index (BMI) of 34.5 kg/m2.

Participants switched from an injectable GLP-1 medication to oral semaglutide between January 5 and February 7, 2026. There was no requirement for how long they had used an injectable medication or how much weight they had lost before switching.

Participants were required to use oral semaglutide regularly for 3 months and self-report their weight within 30 days of starting treatment and again at the end of the study period.

After 3 months of taking oral semaglutide, participants had lost an average of 4.1% of their body weight, or 8.8 pounds.

At the 3-month mark, 2 in 5 participants (40.7%) had lost 5% or more of their body weight.

The proportion of participants with a BMI of 30 or greater also decreased by 21.6 percentage points, from 87.1% at baseline to 65.5% after 3 months.

Most participants (82.4%) reported at least one treatment improvement. Around 69% reported better-fitting clothes, and around 51% reported eating healthier.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Medical Director, Diabetes & Metabolic Center at University Hospitals, Cleveland, OH, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that, “These findings are encouraging because they suggest that some people can continue losing weight after switching to oral treatment.”

However, she also noted, “I would view this as promising early evidence supporting another treatment option, rather than proof that switching improves results.”

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, noted that because the oral medication is absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract, less of it reaches the bloodstream compared to the injectable form.

However, oral semaglutide can still be effective for weight loss.

“While studies show that the injectable form is more efficacious, current findings demonstrate that the oral version is also effective for weight loss,” said Ali.

Some people may prefer the oral form for ease of use and transportation because it does not require refrigeration. However, it must be taken in the morning on an empty stomach, followed by a 30-minute wait before eating, Ali told Healthline.

“Both formulations can cause gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation. Taking a pill does not eliminate those risks,” Hatipoglu said.

Hatipoglu also said factors to consider include how well your current treatment is working, side effects, your comfort with injections, your daily routine, cost, and insurance coverage.

She added that the decision should be made with a prescribing clinician, who can help plan the transition and monitor your response.

“Both options can be effective, so patients should discuss the risks and benefits of each with their provider. Ultimately, these medications are tools to support a healthier diet and lifestyle, and patients who make these fundamental changes achieve the best results,” said Ali.

#4783. Detached Nails More Than 4 Times Higher Among GLP-1 Users, Study Finds

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 users have reported various unusual side effects like “Ozempic feet,” “Ozempic butt,” and “Ozempic breasts.” These changes have been largely tied to rapid weight loss.

Now, fingernails have entered the conversation. Nails detaching from the nail bed or changing color may be more common among people taking GLP-1 drugs, according to a new study. In the study, which researchers presented in October at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026 in Vienna, people taking GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide — Ozempic, Wegovy — and tirzepatide — Mounjaro, Zepbound — reported nail detachment and nail discoloration more often than people who didn’t take the drugs.

When the researchers counted only nail changes that started after treatment began, the link between GLP-1 use and nail detachment nearly disappeared, study author Charles Taïeb, MD, PhD, told Healthline.

“This is why we insist that a substantial part of the nail excess reflects the patients’ overall health rather than the drug itself, while a modest drug-specific effect remains plausible,” Taïeb said.Earlier research has also linked GLP-1 use to hair loss. In the new study, the researchers explained why they examined nails, noting that nails and hair both grow from cells that divide quickly.

However, the researchers cautioned in a press release that the study can’t establish that the drugs caused the nail changes. Both the nail study and a companion hair study captured self-reported symptoms at a single point in time, a design that can identify associations only, they said.

For the study, researchers examined a representative sample of people in France, the United States, Brazil, and Mexico.

Participants included 575 people taking GLP-1 drugs and 1,329 people with type 2 diabetes, obesity, or both conditions, who had never taken GLP-1 drugs.

The average treatment duration was 18.5 months, and researchers tracked weight loss over three months.

They also looked separately at people who had lost weight, to help tell whether the drugs or the weight loss explained the changes. However, the abstract didn’t specify which GLP-1 drugs participants took.

The researchers have submitted the findings to peer-reviewed dermatology journals, where they are under review, Taïeb told Healthline. Here’s what they found.

According to the American Academy of Dermatology (AAD), nail detachment, or onycholysis, occurs when a nail lifts, and the lifted area often appears white.

Taïeb told Healthline that the study asked about “nail detachment” because patients, not doctors, filled out the questionnaire. Nail detachment was the strongest signal among the five nail changes the researchers asked about, Taïeb said.

According to the abstract, 39% of GLP-1 users reported nail separation or detachment (onycholysis), compared with 9% of nonusers.

Nail discoloration is a change in a nail’s usual color, such as white, yellow, or greenish-black, according to the AAD.According to the abstract, 46% of GLP-1 users reported discoloration, compared with 17% of nonusers. Ridges or grooves and fragile nails were also more common among GLP-1 users.

Mir B. Ali, MD, a bariatric surgeon and medical director of the MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Los Angeles, said that while he prescribes GLP-1s, nail detachment hasn’t come up in his practice. Ali wasn’t involved in the research.“I haven’t had anybody complain of that. It’s not something we really see,” he told Healthline. He said his patients more often mention brittle nails or minor changes in nail color.

Over a three-month period, 76% of GLP-1 users reported weight loss, compared with 47% of nonusers, according to the abstract.Weight loss alone didn’t appear to explain the nail findings, the researchers said in the press release. The differences between users and nonusers held up when they looked only at people who had lost weight.The researchers also cautioned in the press release that the study can’t show the drugs caused the changes. They noted that about half of GLP-1 users had nail problems before starting treatment.

Adjusting for skin conditions and nutritional deficiencies weakened some of the associations, they said, though nail detachment and discoloration stayed about two to three times as common among users.Those adjustments relied on conditions participants reported, including iron, vitamin B12, zinc, and vitamin D deficiencies, as well as psoriasis, eczema, and other skin conditions, Taïeb said.“GLP-1 medications may affect the nails indirectly rather than directly,” said Tanya Evans, MD, a board certified dermatologist and medical director of the Skin Cancer Program at the Melanoma Clinic at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, who wasn’t involved in the research.Because the drugs reduce appetite, some people may eat less protein, iron, and zinc, which can contribute to brittle nails, discoloration, or nail detachment, Evans told Healthline. Rapid weight loss may also temporarily disrupt nail growth, much as it can trigger hair shedding, she said.Ali said the total amount of weight a person loses plays a bigger role in hair and nail changes than the rate at which they lose it.

The U.S. labels for Wegovy and Zepbound list hair loss as a side effect reported in clinical trials.

The labels for the Ozempic, both injectable and pill form, as well as Mounjaro, list hair loss as a side effect, based on reports received after the drugs entered the market. Those reports don’t establish how often it happens or whether the drugs caused it.

As such, researchers have been examining GLP-1-related hair loss.

A companion study of the same participants found hair and scalp changes were also more common among GLP-1 users, according to that study’s abstract, also provided to Healthline:

Scalp redness was about three times as common among users, and most users with hair loss also had scalp symptoms such as itching, redness, or scaling.Scalp inflammation may play a role in hair changes among GLP-1 users, in addition to the shedding that often follows rapid weight loss, one of the study’s authors stated in the news release.“This raises the possibility that inflammation may be contributing in some patients, rather than the problem being solely the classic temporary hair shedding associated with rapid weight loss,” Evans said.Experts have told Healthline that hair loss on GLP-1 drugs is often temporary and tied to weight loss.“Hair loss, we see commonly, not only in patients who are on GLP-1 medications, but also in our surgical weight loss patients,” Ali said.

“When you lose weight, especially in women, it releases hormones. You’re getting metabolic changes, and all these things can lead to hair loss and some changes in the nails.” Ali said he tells patients that “as the weight stabilizes at a healthy weight, the hormones stabilize and the hair tends to come back to where it was before.”

Nail detachment and discoloration don’t appear as adverse reactions in the current U.S. prescribing information for Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, or Zepbound.

Ali said the best thing patients can do is get the right nutrition, including enough protein. He said he also advises patients to take a multivitamin along with B-complex, vitamin D, and calcium.

“I would not recommend stopping the GLP-1 medication simply because nail detachment occurs,” Evans said. She advised people to tell their doctor about any new changes in hair, scalp, or nails.Treatment for nail detachment or discoloration depends on the cause, Evans said. A dermatologist can check for an infection, an inflammatory nail disorder, a nutritional problem, an injury, or another explanation, she said.A detached nail recovers as a new nail grows out from its base, Evans said. That takes about 4 to 6 months for a fingernail and 9 to 12 months for a toenail.

Lastly, the AAD recommends having a board certified dermatologist examine any nail that’s lifting.

The AAD also recommends seeing a dermatologist if skin, hair, or nail side effects don’t improve, as they can help determine whether symptoms are due to the medication or another condition.“The important message is don’t panic, but don’t ignore persistent nail changes either,” Evans said.

#4782. What Kids Won't Tell Their Parents

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

November is a good month to be a child in the Gulf. The heat has broken, and families are outside in the evenings for the first time since spring. It is also the point in the school year when the novelty has worn off. Friendship groups have settled, and the first-term report cards are a few weeks away.

For many parents, this is when “How was school?” starts to get the same one-word answer every afternoon: "Fine."

Here in the Gulf, that answer can cover a lot. Our children attend demanding schools in a competitive environment. Their friendship groups shift every year as families arrive and leave, and many of them have been the new child more than once. They are navigating friendship politics and the pressure to do well, and much of it never comes up at home.

This is not unusual, and it is not a sign that something is wrong. Keeping some things private is a normal part of growing up. The more useful question is what leads children to open up.

Two influential studies by Kerr and Stattin (2000) examined how parents come to know about their children’s lives. The common assumption was that parents who ask more questions and keep closer track know more. Instead, the researchers found that parents’ knowledge came mostly from what their children chose to tell them. Spontaneous disclosure, rather than tracking or questioning, predicted how much parents knew, and it was linked to better adjustment in the children themselves.

We cannot question our way into our children’s inner lives. We can only make it more likely that they will let us in.

In our part of the world, there is an additional layer. In my research with Arab families, honor and reputation came up again and again as issues that mattered to young people and their parents, and they were not well captured by the Western measures of family conflict available to us (Rasmi, Daly, & Chuang, 2014). Children in our communities learn early that some things reflect on the whole family and that awareness makes them more careful about what they bring home.

Younger children often do not have the words yet. A 9-year-old who feels left out at school rarely says so. Instead, her parents hear about her stomach ache on a Sunday evening.

One finding from my own work has stayed with me. When we asked young Arab Canadians how they handled disagreements with their parents, the most common approach was to oblige (i.e., to go along with what their parents wanted). On the surface, this looked like the least conflict of all. However, we found, in interviews with emerging adults, that obliging took two distinct forms: Some young people genuinely deferred to their parents, whereas others said yes to their parents’ faces and then quietly did what they had planned anyway (Rasmi, Daly, & Chuang, 2014).

That second group is the one parents need to think about. A child who has learned that disagreement is not safe at home keeps disagreeing but stops telling you about it.

In a follow-up study, we interviewed young people about their relationships with their parents and found that the quality of the relationship shaped almost everything else (Rasmi, Chuang, & Hennig, 2017). Young people talked through their differences when the relationship was close, trusting, and marked by open communication. On the other hand, they withheld information to avoid conflict when they perceived the relationship to be distant or strictly hierarchical. In our quantitative research, a stronger parent–child relationship was also associated with less conflict at home (Rasmi, Chuang, & Hennig, 2015).

Smetana’s research points the same way. Adolescents disclose more to parents they experience as trusting and accepting. Children talk to the parents they feel safe with. That was true of the families I studied in Canada, and it is true of the families we see in Dubai.

Ask smaller questions. “How was your day?” invites one word. “Who did you sit with at lunch?” gives your child somewhere to start.

Talk side by side. Children share more when they are not being looked at directly, and this is the season for it. A walk on the beach after dinner gives you an hour with no screens and no eye contact. Bedtime works, too, when the lights are low.

Watch your reaction. Tilton-Weaver and colleagues (2010) found that when children met negative reactions after sharing something, they shared less afterward. Our response to the lost hoodie tells our children how we will respond to the bigger things.

Make disagreement safe. If your child can tell you they disagree and the conversation stays respectful, they are far more likely to tell you what is actually going on. You can hold your position and still let them voice theirs.

Let silence do some work. Children often circle a difficult topic before they land on it, and if we jump in too soon, they tend to retreat.

Notice what their body is saying. Stomach aches with no medical explanation can be a sign of something unsaid. So can a change in sleep or pulling away from things they used to enjoy. Several together, or any lasting more than a couple of weeks, are worth a gentle conversation and, if needed, a professional.

A child who keeps some things private while otherwise seeming like themselves is doing something healthy. A child who becomes withdrawn or unlike themselves alongside the silence may need more support. The goal is not to know everything, but to be the person your child comes to when it matters.

My colleagues Natalie Maaitah and Valen Valentine and I discussed this on a recent episode of our podcast, Thrive With Us. One idea stayed with me: Connection has to come before correction. Our children only tell us when they have learned that we are safe to tell.

November 20 is World Children’s Day, and its theme, in one form or another, is always listening to children. The cooler months give us more time together than any other part of the year. Some of it can go to smaller questions and to listening to the answers.

Kerr, M., & Stattin, H. (2000). What parents know, how they know it, and several forms of adolescent adjustment: Further support for a reinterpretation of monitoring. Developmental Psychology, 36(3), 366–380. DOI: 10.1037/0012-1649.36.3.366

Rasmi, S., Chuang, S. S., & Hennig, K. (2015). The acculturation gap-distress model: Extensions and application to Arab Canadian families. Cultural Diversity and Ethnic Minority Psychology, 21(4), 630–642. DOI: 10.1037/cdp0000014

Rasmi, S., Chuang, S. S., & Hennig, K. (2017). Seeing eye to eye in Arab Canadian families: Emerging adult perspectives. Journal of Adolescent Research, 32(3), 263–290. DOI: 10.1177/0743558416630814

Rasmi, S., Daly, T. M., & Chuang, S. S. (2014). Intergenerational conflict management in immigrant Arab Canadian families. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 45(7), 1124–1144. DOI: 10.1177/0022022114532358

Smetana, J. G., Metzger, A., Gettman, D. C., & Campione-Barr, N. (2006). Disclosure and secrecy in adolescent–parent relationships. Child Development, 77(1), 201–217. DOI: 10.1111/j.1467-8624.2006.00865.x

Smetana, J. G., Villalobos, M., Tasopoulos-Chan, M., Gettman, D. C., & Campione-Barr, N. (2009). Early and middle adolescents’ disclosure to parents about activities in different domains. Journal of Adolescence, 32(3), 693–713. DOI: 10.1016/j.adolescence.2008.06.010

Stattin, H., & Kerr, M. (2000). Parental monitoring: A reinterpretation. Child Development, 71(4), 1072–1085. DOI: 10.1111/1467-8624.00210

Tilton-Weaver, L., Kerr, M., Pakalniskeine, V., Tokic, A., Salihovic, S., & Stattin, H. (2010). Open up or close down: How do parental reactions affect youth information management? Journal of Adolescence, 33(2), 333–346. DOI: 10.1016/j.adolescence.2009.07.011

#4781. Hyundai launches the new IONIQ 6 in the UK with up to 422 miles of range, starting at $45K

The new Hyundai IONIQ 6 is now on sale in the UK with an impressive range of up to 422 miles, starting at about $45,000.

Hyundai opened orders for the all-new IONIQ 6 in the UK, starting at £33,240 ($45,000), including the Electric Car Grant (ECG).

The “evolved” electrified streamliner brings a sharp new design, a refined interior, and a bigger battery for longer range.

Hyundai “enhanced every line and detail” for a cleaner, stronger silhouette. The front includes a redesigned shark nose and slim daytime running lights, while the black lower body garnish now extends into the doors.

The rear features a new extended ducktail design replacing the previous generation’s prominent spoiler.

Inside, Hyundai overhauled the new IONIQ 6’s interior with a redesigned two-tone leather steering wheel, a digital side mirror, and a “bridge-type” center console that includes a wireless phone charger and physical buttons.

It includes Hyundai’s new infotainment setup, including dual 12.3″ navigation and infotainment screens with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto capabilities.

In the UK, the new IONIQ 6 is available in three trims: Premium, N-Line, and N-Line Evo, with 225 horsepower RWD or 320 horsepower AWD powertrains.

The base Hyundai IONIQ 6 Premium uses a new 84 kWh battery with the 225 hp RWD powertrain, delivering up to 422 miles of range and 4.6 miles/kWh efficiency.

It starts at £33,240 with the ECG. It includes 18″ alloy wheels, flush auto door handles, dual-zone climate control, heated front seats, heated steering wheel, heat pump, smart regenerative braking, wireless phone charging, over-the-air updates, and the full suite of key safety systems.

The IONIQ 6 N-Line starts at £36,240, including the ECG, and adds a more dynamic N-Line exterior and interior design.

Upgrading to the range-topping N-Line Evo costs £43,270 and adds features like leather and suede seat trim, a suede headliner, front relaxation seats, ventilated front seats, an electric sunroof, and a head-up display.

Other added features included with the N-Line Evo trim include Surround View Monitor, Remote Smart Parking Assist, Parking Collision Avoidance Assist, Digital Key 2, Walk-Away Lock, exterior Vehicle-to-Load adaptor, and BOSE premium audio.

Both the IONIQ 6 N-Line and N-Line Evo use the 84 kWh battery, providing up to 364 miles of driving range in RWD and up to 354 miles with the AWD powertrain.

Beautiful car, very efficient and from what I read, very comfortable. I had my eyes set on it, but the small trunk was a dealbreaker for me. So I went for the EV6, which is maybe even more of a stunner (in the eyes of the beholder) but admittedly significantly less efficient.

Thanks to its 800-volt electrical architecture, the IONIQ 6’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes at DC fast-charging speeds of up to 350 kW.

The new IONIQ 6 is now available to order on Hyundai UK’s website, with deliveries set to begin in early 2027.

Sadly, those in the US will miss out on the new-and-improved electrified streamliner. Hyundai is discontinuing the standard IONIQ 6 in the US after the 2026 model year, while the performance N will remain on sale.

#4780. Pain Prevalence Higher in Women, Increases Most Rapidly Before 55

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Women experience a higher prevalence of pain than men across different areas of the body, according to a large global study published October 5 in Nature Medicine.

The analysis, which included more than 6 million people, also found that pain prevalence generally increased with age, with the most rapid increases occurring before age 55.

The findings come as lower back pain, neck pain, and osteoarthritis — all common causes of pain — are projected to become more prevalent globally by 2050.

Pain, especially lower back pain, is the leading cause of disability worldwide. However, researchers have lacked a standardized way to examine how self-reported pain varies across the life span and different regions of the world.

This new study is one of the largest efforts to date to examine self-reported pain using a standardized approach.

The researchers analyzed data from 6,125,459 individuals spanning 118 countries from 1990 to 2025. Participants ranged in age from 5 to more than 100, and 55% were female.

They used self-reported data on pain across 11 body sites:

The researchers found that women consistently reported a higher prevalence of pain across all 11 sites than men.

The largest differences between women and men were in facial pain, headache, and stomach or abdominal pain.

Pain prevalence also increased most rapidly before age 55, especially at musculoskeletal sites such as the hips, back, and knees.

The researchers found that the prevalence of pain varied considerably by body region and differed by age.

Back pain was the most commonly reported, affecting 40% of participants, while facial pain was the least common at 2%.

Neel Anand, MD, a board certified orthopedic spine surgeon and director of the Cedars-Sinai Spine Center in Los Angeles, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained some factors that may contribute to the high prevalence of back pain.

“Our modern lifestyles involve more prolonged sitting, less physical activity, and more time spent looking down at phones, tablets, and computers, all of which can contribute to poor posture and increased stress on the spine,” he said.

“As we get older, the discs between our vertebrae naturally lose moisture and elasticity, making them more vulnerable to degeneration, bulging, and herniation. Excess weight and smoking can accelerate this process,” Anand added.

In addition to pain at individual body sites, the researchers examined three broader measures: any bodily pain, high intensity pain, and generalized pain.

Any bodily pain was defined as pain reported at any site. High intensity pain was defined as an average pain intensity of 7 or higher on a 0–10 scale. Generalized pain was defined as pain occurring in 4 of 5 body regions according to the 2016 fibromyalgia spatial criteria.

The prevalence of any bodily pain increased progressively across the life span, from around 30% at age 5 to 70% among people ages 100 and older. All three pain measures were consistently higher in women than men.

While any bodily pain increased with age, high intensity and generalized pain peaked in mid-to-late life before declining.

High intensity pain peaked around age 50, while generalized pain peaked around age 70.

These different patterns could help identify when prevention and pain management efforts may be most beneficial across the life span.

Vernon Williams, MD, a sports neurologist and founding director of the Center for Sports Neurology and Pain Medicine at Cedars-Sinai Orthopedics and Sports Medicine in Los Angeles, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline there are several signs that pain should be evaluated by a doctor.

“People shouldn’t feel that they simply have to live with pain. I especially recommend talking with a doctor when pain persists, interferes with sleep or daily activities, limits exercise or function, or is accompanied by symptoms such as numbness, tingling, or weakness,” Williams said.

“Persistent pain deserves an evaluation to identify the underlying cause and develop an appropriate treatment plan.”

The researchers found that smoking, obesity, and lower household income together accounted for 18.3% of the global pain burden across all body sites.

People who currently smoked had a modest but consistently higher prevalence of pain across body sites from adolescence through age 65. The strongest association was seen with facial pain.

Obesity was increasingly associated with pain beginning in early adulthood, particularly in weight-bearing joints such as the knees, hips, feet, and ankles.

Lower household income was also associated with a higher prevalence of pain across all body sites beginning in early adulthood. The strongest association was seen with chest pain.

People with the lowest household incomes were more than twice as likely to report chest pain as those with the highest incomes. This difference was greatest in midlife and narrowed at older ages.

Williams noted that medication isn’t the only option for managing pain.

“Regular, appropriately paced exercise can help change how the brain experiences pain, while mindfulness, breathing exercises, adequate sleep, and other behavioral strategies can help the nervous system better regulate the pain response,” he said. “When medication is needed, I encourage patients to discuss non-opioid and non-pharmacologic options with their doctor as part of a comprehensive approach.”

Anand added that, “The best strategy remains prevention and preservation of function: maintaining a healthy weight, strengthening the muscles that support the joints, and avoiding smoking can all help reduce the strain placed on the musculoskeletal system.”

#4779. Measurability Bias, HR Tech, and Work: The Unholy Trinity

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

In its very design, industrial/organizational (I/O) psychology (a.k.a. "psychology of work") reveals something nuanced and supremely relevant about what drives behavior in organizations.

Industrial psychology treats the individual as the unit of measure, while organizational psychology measures the group. The former tends to be measured quantitatively, while the latter tends to be measured qualitatively.

So, what falls on the “I” side (selection, training, performance management, core human resources [HR]) is very different than what falls on the “O” side (leadership, motivation, organizational development, culture).

From a technological investment point of view, “I” has a lot going for it. For starters, only quantitative data flows cleanly into a system of record, so there’s a built-in motivation for organizational use. But that’s not even the half of it.

Measurability bias describes the tendency of people to prioritize easily quantifiable metrics over qualitative factors that are difficult, if not impossible, to measure.

It’s not hard to understand why. Easily quantifiable metrics require a lot less thinking and ostensibly provide a lot more certainty. (Of course, “ostensibly” is necessary because they’re so often applied incorrectly.)

Human beings hate uncertainty at a cellular level, and we often embrace whatever we can to reassure ourselves that we are making the right decision. This tendency is heightened in professional settings because the stakes are so high. We go out of our way to leverage quantitative data for guidance, cover, and reassurance.

That’s why “I” gets the prize, and it’s not hard to see why. According to analysis by 451 Research, less than 2 percent of sales of the $94 billion HR technology market goes to the qualitatively measured “O” constructs.

The same is true for investment. HRO Today tracked investment in 2025 and found that nearly all of the $3.75 billion went into the “I” side.

And where the technology and investment go, so goes the human attention.

As a result, constructs like leadership, motivation, and organizational culture receive comparably tiny resources and attention. Even something squarely on the “O” side like employee engagement, which had a brief run as the HR metric du jour, only did so because it offered a quantitative measure of a qualitative construct.

If the bias for easily quantifiable metrics creates a disincentive to pursue qualitative constructs through technology and investment, can we at least assume that the upside is that we’re making great decisions, grounded in data and analytics? Nope.

What does the peer-reviewed research say about the efficacy of HR technology and investment on the “I” side of I/O psychology? There’s not a lot of it. What we do know isn’t promising.

Hiring? Research from Bauer and SHRM (2010) indicates that half of senior hires fail within 18 months, and that 50 percent of hourly workers leave within the first 120 days.

Training? A study by Saks and Belcourt (2006) found that two out of three trainees were not using the training one year later.

One could argue that HR technology has adopted these same practices and merely reproduced them at greater scale, as Capelli did in his HBR article (2019).

Performance management? Scullen, Mount, and Goff (2000) found that between 53 and 62 percent of variance in feedback is reflective of the feedback provider, not the feedback recipient. In other words, the feedback tells us more about the person providing it than the person receiving it. Kluger and DeNisi (1996) found that feedback actually harms performance more than a third of the time.

That research may be dated, but it reveals something fundamental about human behavior that performance management still fails to take into account.

There’s an ironic twist, to boot. What gets in the way of the efficacy of the heavily weighted technological investment in industrial psychology driven by measurement bias? Measurement bias.

What gets measured in selection? Volume of applications and time to fill. What doesn’t get measured? Outcomes. For training, it’s completion and satisfaction. And most performance management efforts have little to do with performance.

We don’t measure the outcomes of hiring decisions because it’s too hard to do and takes way too long. The same is true for training outcomes. By the time we know, we think (incorrectly) it’s too late to do anything about it. And performance management? The logical overriding motivation for managers is not to hurt anyone’s motivation moving forward, and that's not what performance management is designed to do.

Concerns about the effect of artificial intelligence (AI) on people and work are as well-founded as they are widespread. But they also overlook how AI can help us to be more human.

The ability to analyze qualitative data sets at a breakneck speed means that practitioners finally have access to the types of evidence that provide demonstrable proof of impact and return on investment (ROI).

Proper use of AI can tell us more about leadership, motivation, and culture at an organization than we have ever known. And it can do so in ways that support great decision-making, both strategically and tactically.

Our company is designing HR tools that can provide the benefits of psychological safety (surfacing truth) where it does not exist. We achieve this by summarizing anonymous qualitative data in real time, carefully framing the summary to avoid finger-pointing and surfacing the most productive steps forward.

We accelerate team decision-making by summarizing everyone’s opinion before the conversation begins, using pre-surfaced conflicting points of view as the starting point for discussions. We use AI to nudge people into creating better and more aligned goals across the organization. And now we can surface the way work really gets done through a combination of AI-document reviews and AI-assisted human-led interviews.

These are but a few examples of how AI can revolutionize HR and HR tech: by creating better sources of qualitative data. It may sound abstract, but the positive effect on work will be profound.

Yes, the impact that AI can have on the future of work is very scary. But interestingly, it also just might make the future of work way more human.

#4778. Taking Blood Pressure Meds? DASH Diet Likely Safe for Potassium Levels

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who adhere to the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet do not experience significant changes in potassium levels while taking blood pressure medications or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) drugs, according to a new study.

Researchers also reported that people taking these medications do not experience significant changes in their kidney function.

Both types of medications are known to increase potassium levels. High potassium levels can lead to hyperkalemia, a condition that can cause issues with the heart rhythm. People with impaired kidney function due to chronic kidney disease are at increased risk of hyperkalemia.

“The DASH diet is a well-known, proven nutrition pattern that is known to improve blood pressure,” said Marian Budu, MD, a clinical research coordinator on the GoFresh Trials at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston and the presenting author of the study, in a news release.

“Knowing that the DASH diet did not increase blood potassium levels in this population with normal baseline potassium levels provides assurance that the DASH diet can be prescribed to a wide range of people,” she continued.

The preliminary findings are being presented at the American Heart Association’s Hypertension Scientific Sessions 2026 meeting this week in Virginia. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the research provides medical professionals with important information.

“While we have traditionally exercised caution before recommending the DASH diet in patients who are prescribed ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, or potassium-sparing diuretics, these results show that those patients could likely adopt the DASH diet without significant concern for harm,” said Cheng-Han Chen, MD, an interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA.

“DASH diets do not appear to increase potassium levels to any significant degree in patients taking medications that are known to potentially raise serum potassium,” added Kevin Volpp, MD, the founding director of the Penn Center for Health Incentives and Behavioral Economics in Pennsylvania and the scientific lead of the American Heart Association’s Health Care by Food initiative.

“This is important because it is a theoretical concern that diets rich in potassium could cause high levels in potassium in some patients.”

The new study was a secondary analysis of the GoFresh and GoFresh Rx randomized trials that enrolled Black adults in the greater Boston area with high blood pressure.

Some of the participants were taking medications to lower their blood pressure, and others were not taking any hypertension drugs.

The study focused on four classes of blood pressure medications: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and potassium-sparing diuretics and beta-blockers, as well as NSAIDs.

The analysis took place in 2026 and included 356 Black adults with an average age of 53. About 70% were women.

At the start of the study, the participants had systolic blood pressure readings between 120 mm Hg and less than 150 mm Hg. They also had a diastolic blood pressure reading of less than 100 mm Hg.

The participants also had varying degrees of kidney function. In addition, they had limited access to grocery stores.

Half of the participants received three months of weekly DASH-patterned groceries and weekly nutrition counseling sessions. The other half received a cash stipend every four weeks to buy groceries, with no nutrition counseling.

The participants’ blood potassium levels were measured at the beginning of the study and again after 12 weeks.

The researchers reported that eating more potassium-rich foods in the DASH diet did not increase potassium levels to dangerous levels among participants taking blood pressure medications.

They noted no significant increase in potassium levels, regardless of whether participants were assigned to the dietary intervention or the monetary stipend group.

In a news release, the researchers acknowledged that their study did not include people with stage 4 or stage 5 kidney disease or those with higher-than-normal potassium levels.

They added that the study population comprised only Black individuals living in Boston, so the results may not generalize to the broader population.

The study authors said that future research should focus on participants with suboptimal kidney function and those with higher potassium levels.

Volpp agreed that more research is needed.

“This study was conducted in patients with non-elevated potassium levels at baseline and does not answer the question of whether they are safe in patients with elevated potassium levels or significant impairments in renal function,” he told Healthline.

Chen noted that potassium levels should be taken seriously.

“Certain classes of blood pressure medications can potentially cause high potassium levels, especially in people with kidney disease,” he told Healthline. “If potassium levels become too high, this can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, nausea, and muscle pain, or even serious heart problems such as arrhythmias.”

The DASH diet is a dietary plan that emphasizes fruits, vegetables, and lean proteins such as chicken, fish, and beans.

The plan also includes whole grains, low fat dairy products, and cooking with vegetable oils. The diet discourages the intake of red meat, salt, fat, and added sugars.

Previous research has indicated that the DASH diet can provide numerous health benefits.

A preliminary 2022 study concluded that the dietary plan can help lower blood pressure and improve heart health, but those results haven’t been published in a scientific journal. Still, the findings were consistent with a 2019 study that found the DASH diet can help lower the risk of heart disease.

In addition, a 2020 study reported that adults aged 65 and older with obesity lost body fat while following the DASH Diet. A 2023 study suggested the diet can help reduce belly fat.

A 2019 meta-analysis suggested that the DASH diet may also help lower the risk of certain cancers.

Many of these protective effects are attributed to the diet’s high fruit and vegetable content.

Chen said the DASH diet has many benefits, but the eating plan might not be for everybody.

“The DASH diet has been shown to be beneficial in lowering blood pressure, losing weight, and controlling blood sugar and cholesterol levels,” he said. “However, the amount of planning and portion tracking required to follow the diet may be too much for some people.”

Chen recommended that people ease into the DASH diet.

“The best way to start on the DASH diet is to slowly introduce the changes to your meals,” he said. “This can be as simple as including a few extra servings of fruits and vegetables each day as well as swapping some whole grain products for refined grains. Over time, more of the diet can be incorporated.”

Volpp agreed that introducing the DASH diet in increments is a good strategy.

“For many people, it is easiest to make small incremental changes sequentially,” he said. “One way to get started is to increase fruit by a couple of servings a day. Another is to pay attention to the amount of sodium in packaged foods and consciously choose products lower in sodium. A third is to make a conscious effort to eat more vegetables.”

“Make changes first that are easiest for you to make; it will be easier to make those changes stick,” Volpp added.

#4777. The Jeep Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept Is a High-Speed Desert-Shredding Machine

But don’t be too surprised to see something like this concept reach showrooms in the next few years.

The Jeep CJ-8 Scrambler of the 1980s took the basic CJ-7, stretched it, and added a pickup bed. Jeep’s latest concept, the Wrangler Scrambler SRT, takes that same formula and ups the ante. Unveiled at the 2026 Specialty Equipment Market Association (SEMA) Show, the Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept is not just a body kit on top of a Wrangler frame. Instead, the Wrangler-based concept is the beginning of new developments for the off-road brand, particularly in suspension technology.

The highlight of the concept model is a bespoke high-travel independent front suspension, developed with off-road racing champion Casey Currie. The all-new suspension expands the concept’s performance envelope with enhanced steering precision, wheel control, and high-speed stability. Jeep also added a trophy-truck-inspired rear axle, heavy-duty wheel package, and desert-racing-informed hardware to ensure long-term durability. The suspension architecture first appeared on the Jeep Striker Concept, and was validated by Currie in a custom Jeep Gladiator “Striker” at the NORRA 500.

“The original Scrambler became an icon because it broke the rules. It looked different, worked differently and represented a certain kind of freedom that resonated with enthusiasts then and still does today,” said Tim Kuniskis, head of American brands, SRT Performance, and Direct Connection, Stellantis North America. “We asked ourselves a more provocative question: what happens when SRT stops treating the trail as the limit and builds the ultimate open-air desert weapon? The Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept is our answer.”

Jeep may have started with a Wrangler chassis, but the final product is not dimensionally similar to a factory JL-generation model. Behind the A-pillar, Jeep added longer doors, custom rear bodywork, an integrated pickup bed, a redesigned tailgate, unique fender flares, and a structural roll cage. Up front, the Wrangler Scrambler features a sharknose design like the Gladiator. (We can’t help but smile at the Punk’n orange paint and bronze-painted beadlock wheels.)

Inside the Wrangler Scrambler, Jeep focused on adaptability. That’s why the rear seats clip securely into floor-mounted hooks and can be removed entirely or rotated to create rear-facing seating. Removing the rear seats allows for storing camping gear, motorcycles, and other adventure equipment without compromise. Dark Graphite leather, orange inserts, contrast stitching, bronze accents, and SRT embroidery adorn the touchpoints of the interior.

Jeep didn’t specify which engine the Scrambler Wrangler uses or detail power figures, but the automaker did leave us some clues about its powertrain. The concept model “honors the original Scrambler” by “imagining how far its rule-breaking formula could be pushed when V-8 power, desert-racing hardware, and SRT performance development are allowed to run without constraint.” That sure sounds like a V-8 engine is under the hood. We’ll cross our fingers that it’s the supercharged 6.2-liter unit out of the Hellcat lineup.

“The Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept combines everything enthusiasts love about Jeep vehicles—capability, open-air freedom and authenticity—with the power, control and relentless performance mindset that define SRT,” Kuniskis said. “It is overbuilt and engineered around the idea that the desert can be every bit as demanding as a racetrack. It is unapologetic by design.”

And while this may seem like a flight of SEMA fancy, we suspect it may be a tease for a production car to come. After all, Stellantis’s wide-ranging brand presentation back in May said the carmaker was planning a 2-door Wrangler Scrambler pickup, and that said vehicle would also have an SRT version...

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4776. Why Do We Love Some Accents and Hate Others?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

We all have personal opinions about certain accents. Some make us swoon, while others make us cringe. They seem to inspire remarkably strong reactions for something as ordinary as the way a person pronounces their words.

To many people’s ears, a French accent might sound sophisticated and seductive, while a German accent is sometimes described as harsh or angry. A British accent may suggest refinement and education, but depending on where in Britain it comes from, it could also attract assumptions about someone’s intelligence or social class.

However, our reactions to accents often reveal more about our own prejudices than the people speaking. And these judgments aren't harmless: Accent bias can affect how people are perceived and treated.

An accent is the way we pronounce words that is influenced by our regional and social backgrounds. Everyone has one, although some people mistakenly believe they speak without an accent and that it’s everyone else who has one.

Accents carry powerful social associations and biases. (Stollznow, 2026) Perhaps the best-known example in British English is Received Pronunciation (RP), better known as the Queen’s English (now the King’s English) or BBC English. Popularized through the BBC’s newsreaders and presenters in the 1920s, this accent became associated with education, wealth, authority, and social privilege. To many people, it still sounds like the voice of someone who knows what they’re talking about.

But not all accents enjoy this same prestige. The Southern U.S. accent is sometimes unfairly associated with a lack of education, intelligence, or sophistication, reflecting longstanding stereotypes about the American South. Yet such perceptions depend on the context. In some communities, a Southern drawl might signal warmth, friendliness, authenticity, and regional pride. The same accent that one listener dismisses as unsophisticated might be valued by another as a marker of identity and belonging. Linguists call this covert prestige. This is the social value attached to ways of speaking that might not be considered prestigious by wider society, but are highly prized within particular communities.

Accent prejudice can also reflect much deeper social inequalities. African American English, for example, has long been stigmatized through racist stereotypes associating its speakers with laziness, poor education, and criminality. (Barrett, et al., 2022) These judgments have little to do with the dialect itself and everything to do with the prejudices faced by this group of people. Within this community, however, African American English is an important marker of identity, solidarity, and cultural pride. Its influence on jazz, R&B, hip hop, and popular culture also demonstrates its considerable cultural prestige beyond the community.

Our reactions to accents aren’t always about social class or race. Sometimes, we simply decide subjectively that certain languages sound more beautiful while others sound unpleasant (Crystal, 2014). For instance, French has a longstanding reputation as the language of love. Its associations with romance, fashion, fine dining, and literature have helped cement its image as elegant and sophisticated. Its rhythm, nasal vowels, and soft consonants contribute to the impression of musicality. There’s even a popular notion that everything sounds better in French, including insults. In The Matrix Reloaded, the Merovingian declares, “I have sampled every language. French is my favorite—a fantastic language, especially to curse with.” He then launches into a string of obscenities. It’s an unconventional endorsement, but it captures the seductive reputation that French has acquired.

The German language often gets a less flattering reception. It’s regularly described as harsh, guttural, or aggressive. The Irish comedian Dylan Moran once joked that German “sounds like a typewriter eating tinfoil being kicked down the stairs.” Its consonant clusters and sharp sounds might contribute to this impression, but our reactions are also affected by cultural stereotypes. German speakers are sometimes portrayed as cold, rigid, and overly concerned with rules and order. Historical associations with World War II and Nazi Germany have also influenced negative perceptions of the language. These stereotypes have a long history. The 16th-century Holy Roman Emperor Charles V once said that he spoke Spanish to God, Italian to women, French to men, and German to his horse.

Of course, French isn’t inherently romantic, and German isn’t naturally angry. No accent is objectively more intelligent, attractive, or pleasant than any other. These impressions are learned, reinforced by cultural representations, historical associations, media portrayals, and even our own personal experiences with the accent.

What sounds sophisticated to one listener might sound pretentious to someone else. What sounds friendly and familiar to one person might sound provincial to another. These judgments can have serious real-world consequences. Accent prejudice can influence hiring decisions, education, healthcare and legal outcomes, social relationships, and how much credibility we give someone. We might like to think we’re judging people based on what they say, but sometimes we’re making up our minds before we’ve even heard their point of view.

Perhaps the next time we find ourselves admiring or disliking someone’s accent, it’s worth considering what we’re really responding to. Is it the sounds themselves, or the stories, stereotypes, and biases we’ve attached to them?Learn more in my new book, Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language.

Stollznow, K. 2026. Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language. Cambridge University Press.

Barrett, R., Cramer, J., & McGowan, K. B. 2023. English With an Accent: Language, Ideology, and Discrimination in the United States. Routledge.

Crystal, D., & Crystal, B. 2014. You Say Potato: The Story of English Accents. Pan Macmillan.

#4775. Tested: 2026 GMC Sierra 1500 Denali Ultimate Duramax: Oil’s Well That Ends Well

A turbodiesel inline-six proves a nice match for GMC’s fanciest half-ton pickup, especially if road trips or towing are in the cards.

Luxury pickup trucks, once quite the oxymoron, have exploded into popularity in the last decade or so. Truckmakers formerly content simply to one-up each other on power, torque, or towing capacity are now engaged in battles over the nicest materials, the most potent stereos, the flashiest in-car tech, and the most comfortable seats.

But what’s under the hood still matters for many buyers, especially those who plan on using their trucks for work as well as play. Plenty of vehicles can do luxury, plenty of them can haul loads. But nailing both of those at the same time takes skill.

The GMC Sierra Denali has more experience at that than anything else on the road, having first landed in dealerships back in 2001. There is, as you might have heard, a newly face-lifted Sierra set to arrive shortly, but unlike the heavy-duty models, the turbodiesel engine in 1500s doesn’t change. So if you care more about torque than having the latest infotainment, look for these 2026 versions on the lot; you might find one for a deal.

The GMC Sierra is one of America’s best-selling vehicles. Alone, it racked up more than 348,000 sales in America in 2025, more than the Toyota Camry or Tesla Model Y; add in its effective twin, the Chevrolet Silverado, and that number crested 925,000 last year alone. It’s been the keystone of the GMC lineup since 1968, offering a slightly more upscale alternative to the Chevy and delivering the full variety of beds, engines, body styles and beyond that buyers have come to expect from pickups.The 1500 designation marks this as the mainstream light-duty pickup (formerly known as “half-ton”), versus the heavy-duty 2500, 3500, and beyond. Denali is GMC’s highly successful premium subbrand; the suffix Ultimate marks the recently added top trim within the Denali line, which piles on even more high-end features. Duramax is GM’s in-house term for the diesel engines used in its beefiest trucks and SUVs. Here, it refers to a turbocharged inline-six shared with the Silverado 1500, as well as the GMC Yukon and Chevrolet Tahoe/Suburban.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

Vehicle Tested: 2026 GMC Sierra 1500 Denali UltimateBase Price: $87,195Price as Tested: $89,204Test Location: New York/Vermont

Engine: 2992-cc turbocharged diesel inline-six

0–60 mph: 6.8 sec (Hearst Autos, similar model)

Transmission: 10-speed automatic, four-wheel drive

EPA Fuel Economy (City/Highway/Combined): 22/26/24 mpg

GM’s pickup trucks tend to sit at the front of the class in terms of driving dynamics—not that many actual buyers are likely to care, but we at Road & Track certainly do. Pay attention, and you’ll notice a level of fidelity coming through the wheel that Ford’s, Toyota’s, and Ram’s pickups lack; there’s a comparative crispness, a little extra reward for the enthusiast forced to drive a body-on-frame brute. But let’s face it, nobody would choose a pickup based on steering feel or lateral handling, so even if they’re appreciated, these aspects are largely academic.

The big news here is the turbodiesel engine. It’s notable because GM is the last truckmaker in America still selling an oil-burner in its mainstream light-duty pickups, Ford and Dodge Ram having given up a few years back. Their loss is the General’s gain, though. The Duramax suits the truck’s nature well, delivering a smooth rush of midrange power that makes highway driving breezy. The top end may be lacking compared with a burly gas-powered V-8, but down in the meat of the powerband, where most of the real work gets done, the turbodiesel provides an immediate, forceful shove that both instils confidence and handily pushes the Sierra past slow-moving traffic.

The biggest appeal of diesel power for truck drivers (and those weird Germans who tried building turbodiesel performance cars back in the Aughts) is low-end torque, and that’s certainly true here. In spite of a displacement of less than 3000 cc, this motor cranks out more torque than the 6.2-liter gasoline engine in the GM pickup line; in fact, it’s only 6 lb-ft behind even the brand-new 6.6-liter V-8. Plus, not only does it generate its full twist at just 2750 rpm, it’s also making 94 percent of that by 1500 rpm, so the force comes up quickly as you roll up from idle.

The motor is unexpectedly quiet for both a truck and a diesel, a trait that plays well with the Denali’s luxury mission. What engine noise does penetrate the cabin comes across with enough inline-six smoothness that I was able to convince myself for a moment that the motor there has some deep ties to the straight-sixes of Germany. (Ironically, the Silverado and Sierra’s gas-powered inline-four sounds more like a traditional diesel than the Duramax from inside the cabin.)

But diesels also generally see better efficiency, in no small part due to the fuel’s greater energy density than good old-fashioned gasoline. The EPA says the blocky Sierra will run 26 mpg on the highway, and I even saw the onboard fuel-economy gauge reach as high as 28.7 mpg on a long highway stretch, a number I’d be happy to see out of many sedans when doing 70-plus mph.

Like any new full-size crew-cab truck, it’s incredibly capable, as long as you have the space to park it. I split my week with the Sierra between New York City and Vermont, and you can probably guess which felt like a better fit.

Checking the Denali Ultimate box—instead of the one named solely after Alaska’s highest peak, without the superlative—means all the bells and all the whistles, many of which are appreciated but others a little extraneous. Power-folding steps and Super Cruise are handy, 22-inch chrome wheels perhaps less so. But at the end of the day, if you add up the standard features that are options on the regular Denali, you’re paying around $5000 for blacked-out chrome and nicer interior materials.

Admittedly, these are nice materials. I was impressed with the Alpine Umber full-grain-leather upholstery, which looks worthy of use on Filson jackets or lingering glances from the camera in a Taylor Sheridan show. Same goes for the trim, especially the open-pore wood used nearly as expansively as in your typical Bentley. And the topographic map-style details in both also add nuance to the cabin, helping it better justify its price point.

(Do note that the 2027 Sierra 1500 Denali Ultimate exclusively adopts both a black-on-black interior and lots of additional screen real estate, leaving the outgoing model’s Western warmth behind for clinical urban cool. If you like the current look, go for the ’26 or look elsewhere.)

While the back seats’ biggest advantage is S-Class–worthy legroom, the fronts deserve greater praise. Nicely padded and equipped with heating, ventilation, and a pleasant massage function, they are perfect for road trips using GM’s class-leading Super Cruise hands-free driving assist and a fuel tank large enough to enable 500-plus-mile highway stints without seeing a warning light.Of course, there is the elephant in the room: the cost of diesel. As of this story, it’s around $6.50 per gallon on average. Fill-ups for a Sierra Duramax are liable to run $130 or so for the average American, and even for folks buying near-$100K pickups, seeing those sorts of numbers on a gas-pump display is likely to induce some heartburn.

The Sierra 1500 Denali Ultimate’s clearest rival at the top of the fancy-pants truck market is the Ram 1500 Tungsten; Chevy, Ford, and Toyota also offer their own top truck trims—Silverado High Country, F-150 Platinum, Tundra Capstone—but while they make for great places to knock out the miles, their cabins can’t quite equal the front-runners. The Ram’s Hurricane engine is in some ways a gas-powered analogue to the Duramax, displacing almost the exact same amount of air and delivering more power and torque while not requiring any of the minor annoyances of diesel life. Add in the Mopar’s nicer interior and air-ride suspension, and it’s hard not to see it as the better choice for those rare truck buyers without a brand allegiance—but the GMC feels like a solid silver medalist in this particular competition.Ask for the diesel-versus-gas debate, much of it comes down to how much weight you tow, how often you tow that sort of weight, and even where you tow it. If the loads you pull close in on the truck’s 8800-pound maximum, or if you’re doing it often at altitudes where the turbodiesel’s forced induction pays dividends over GM’s naturally aspirated V-8s, then the Duramax probably sounds awfully appealing.

If you tow a lot, or if you take a lot of long road trips where you’d rather go farther without stopping and truck stops abound along your routes, I’d say diesel is the better choice. (If nothing else, you’ll avoid any worries at the back of your mind about V-8 engine reliability.)

The pockets inside the rear bench. Much to the delight of fans of both the Second and Fourth Amendments, General Motors has long packed its large SUVs and trucks in particular with hidey-holes for handheld objects (hell, not just SUVs and trucks; even the C7 Corvette had a secret stash spot behind the infotainment screen), but the Sierra Denali’s back-seat storage spaces are large enough to be significantly more usable than any wallet-sized cubbyhole, while still being secret enough to go unnoticed if you tuck in their pull tabs.
